title: Telling a story: aspect in narration
objectives: I can tell a story in the past, with perfective verbs for the chain of events and imperfective verbs for the background, for habits and for an action that another one interrupts.
I can link events with 'коли́', 'по́ки' and 'як ті́льки', and choose the aspect each of them calls for.
I can say how long something took, how long it lasted and how much later it happened with 'за', 'протя́гом' and 'че́рез', and tell the three apart.
I can tell a life story: where someone was born and grew up, where they studied and settled, and when they got married.
I can explain how 'ви́ріс', 'дити́нство', 'пам’ята́ти' and 'знайшо́в' are spelled and pronounced.

vocabulary.note: Past 'поме́р', 'поме́рла', 'поме́рли'; future 'помру́', 'помре́ш', in which the 'е' of the infinitive drops out. Imperfective partner 'помира́ти'. It is the neutral word for a death in a life story, the counterpart of 'народи́тися' from the unit on numerals.

example.target: Мій діду́сь поме́р, коли́ мені́ було́ де́сять ро́ків.
example.source: My grandpa died when I was ten.
example.source_literal: My grandpa died, when to-me was ten of-years.

vocabulary.note: Imperfective partner 'виро́стати'. Future 'ви́росту', 'ви́ростеш'; past 'ви́ріс', 'ви́росла', 'ви́росли'. The perfective prefix 'ви-' is stressed in every form. The verb without the prefix, 'рости́', means 'to grow': 'росли́ ви́шні', cherry trees grew.

example.source: My children grew up in Kyiv.

vocabulary.note: Imperfective partner 'вступа́ти'. Future 'вступлю́', 'всту́пиш', with 'л' added after 'п' as in 'куплю́'. 'Вступи́ти до університе́ту', literally 'to enter to university', means to be admitted to a university and begin studying there: 'до' with the genitive.

example.source: My sister got into university.

vocabulary.note: Imperfective partner 'оселя́тися'. It means to make a place one's home for good, and takes 'в' or 'у' with the locative. Past 'осели́вся', 'осели́лася', 'осели́лися'.

example.target: Пі́сля університе́ту вони́ осели́лися у Льво́ві.
example.source: After university they settled in Lviv.

vocabulary.note: Imperfective partner 'одру́жуватися'. The partner is 'з' with the instrumental: 'одружи́тися з Мико́лою'. The same verb serves for a man and for a woman, and in the plural, with no partner named, it means that two people married each other.

example.source: My brother got married in the summer.

vocabulary.note: Imperfective partner 'знахо́дити' ('знахо́джу', 'знахо́диш'). Its forms are built like those of 'іти́': future 'знайду́', 'зна́йдеш'; past 'знайшо́в', 'знайшла́', 'знайшли́'. It names the result of a search; the search itself is 'шука́ти'.

example.source: Oksana found her keys.

vocabulary.note: Imperfective partner 'втрача́ти'. The 'т' becomes 'ч' in the 'я' form: 'втра́чу', 'втра́тиш'. It is used for things, time, work and hope alike. After a consonant, after a comma and at the start of a sentence it is written 'утра́тити' ('Він утра́тив ключ.'), by the euphony rule for 'у' and 'в'. For a thing that has been mislaid, people also say 'загуби́ти'.

example.source: I lost a lot of time.

vocabulary.note: It has no perfective partner with this meaning: 'запам’ята́ти' means 'to memorize'. It takes the accusative, 'про' with the accusative, or a clause with 'що'. It comes from the noun 'па́м’ять', memory.

example.target: Я до́бре пам’ята́ю свою́ пе́ршу вчи́тельку.
example.source: I remember my first teacher well.
example.source_literal: I well remember own first teacher.

vocabulary.note: Imperfective partner 'забува́ти'. Future 'забу́ду', 'забу́деш', like 'бу́ду'; past 'забу́в', 'забу́ла'. 'Забу́ти про' with the accusative is to forget about something; 'забу́ти' with a thing and a place is to leave it behind there by mistake.

example.source: Taras left his key at home.

vocabulary.note: It takes the accusative, with no preposition where English says 'for'. 'Шука́ти' and 'знайти́' are not an aspect pair, but they work as the effort and its result: 'Я шука́в, але́ не знайшо́в.', I looked but did not find it.

example.source: What are you looking for?

vocabulary.note: Built on the root of 'дити́на', child, and stressed on the same syllable. 'У дити́нстві' means 'in childhood', 'as a child'.

example.target: У дити́нстві я жила́ в селі́.
example.source: As a child I lived in a village.
example.source_literal: In childhood I lived in village.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'мо́лодості'. It names the time of being young, from the adjective 'молоди́й'. 'У мо́лодості' means 'when one was young'.

example.target: У мо́лодості мій та́то грав на гіта́рі.
example.source: When he was young, my dad played the guitar.
example.source_literal: In youth my dad played on guitar.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'спо́гаду', plural 'спо́гади'. It is one remembered scene or event; the ability to remember is 'па́м’ять'. 'Спо́гади про' with the accusative are memories of something, and 'спо́гади' is also the word for written memoirs.

example.target: У ме́не є до́брі спо́гади про шко́лу.
example.source: I have good memories of school.
example.source_literal: At me is good memories about school.

vocabulary.note: The story of a person's life, written by another person or, in an application or a class, by oneself.

example.source: I read a biography of Lesya Ukrainka.

vocabulary.note: It joins an action that went on for the whole time of another, so its verb is imperfective. 'По́ки не' with a perfective verb means 'until', and the word 'не' there negates nothing.

example.source: While I was asleep, someone called.

vocabulary.note: Two words, 'як', how, and 'ті́льки', only, used together as one conjunction. The main action follows at once, so the verb after it is perfective.

example.target: Як ті́льки я закі́нчу робо́ту, я тобі́ подзвоню́.
example.source: As soon as I finish work, I'll call you.
example.source_literal: How only I will-finish work, I to-you will-call.

vocabulary.note: It takes the genitive. It belongs mostly to careful speech and writing; in everyday speech a length of time in the accusative alone says the same ('Я чека́в годи́ну.').

example.source: It rained throughout the week.

vocabulary.note: It introduces an unexpected event, so its verb is usually perfective.

example.source: Suddenly someone said my name.

vocabulary.note: It places an event some time after the one just told, often after a long or unstated time. 'По́тім' says only 'next'.

example.target: Споча́тку вона́ працюва́ла в кафе́, а зго́дом ста́ла лі́каркою.
example.source: At first she worked in a café, and later she became a doctor.
example.source_literal: At-first she worked in café, and later became by-doctor.

vocabulary.note: It means 'at that time', and in a story also 'then', the next step. In the first meaning it often comes with an imperfective verb or with 'було́'.

example.source: I was seven then.

dialogues.title: How Halyna met Mykola
dialogues.context: Sam is having tea at the home of Oksana's parents, Halyna and Mykola. Sam says 'ви' to them; they say 'ти' to him. Speaking of Mykola, Sam calls him 'пан Мико́ла', here in the instrumental after 'з': 'з па́ном Мико́лою'. 'Одного́ ве́чора', one evening, and 'ко́жного ве́чора', every evening, are genitives of time, like 'мину́лого ти́жня'.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Па́ні Гали́но, а як ви познайо́милися з па́ном Мико́лою?
lines.source: Ms. Halyna, how did you and Mr. Mykola meet?
lines.source_literal: Ms. Halyna, and how you got-acquainted with Mr. Mykola?

lines.speaker: Гали́на
lines.target: Це було́ два́дцять шість ро́ків тому́. Мені́ тоді́ було́ два́дцять два ро́ки.
lines.source: That was twenty-six years ago. I was twenty-two then.
lines.source_literal: This was twenty six of-years ago. To-me then was twenty two years.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: І де ви тоді́ жили́?
lines.source: And where were you living then?
lines.source_literal: And where you then lived?

lines.speaker: Гали́на
lines.target: У Льво́ві. Я працюва́ла в бібліоте́ці, а Мико́ла був студе́нтом.
lines.source: In Lviv. I worked at a library, and Mykola was a student.
lines.source_literal: In Lviv. I worked in library, and Mykola was by-student.

lines.speaker: Мико́ла
lines.target: Я ходи́в до бібліоте́ки ко́жного ве́чора.
lines.source: I went to the library every evening.
lines.source_literal: I went to library of-every of-evening.

lines.speaker: Гали́на
lines.target: Він сиді́в бі́ля вікна́ й чита́в. Ми не говори́ли.
lines.source: He would sit by the window and read. We didn't talk.
lines.source_literal: He sat by window and read. We not talked.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А що було́ по́тім?
lines.source: And what happened next?
lines.source_literal: And what was then?

lines.speaker: Гали́на
lines.target: Одного́ ве́чора, по́ки я шука́ла для ньо́го кни́гу, він ра́птом запита́в: «У вас є час у субо́ту?»
lines.source: One evening, while I was looking for a book for him, he suddenly asked, 'Are you free on Saturday?'
lines.source_literal: Of-one of-evening, while I searched for him book, he suddenly asked: 'At you is time in Saturday?'

lines.speaker: Мико́ла
lines.target: І вона́ сказа́ла «так»!
lines.source: And she said yes!

lines.speaker: Гали́на
lines.target: У субо́ту ми пішли́ в кіно́, а по́тім до́вго гуля́ли в па́рку.
lines.source: On Saturday we went to the movies, and then we walked in the park for a long time.
lines.source_literal: In Saturday we went in cinema, and then long strolled in park.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А коли́ ви одружи́лися?
lines.source: And when did you get married?
lines.source_literal: And when you got-married?

lines.speaker: Гали́на
lines.target: Че́рез рік, улі́тку. А зго́дом ми осели́лися в Ки́єві.
lines.source: A year later, in the summer. And later we settled in Kyiv.
lines.source_literal: Through year, in-summer. And later we settled in Kyiv.

lines.speaker: Мико́ла
lines.target: А че́рез два ро́ки в нас народи́лася Окса́на.
lines.source: And two years later we had Oksana.
lines.source_literal: And through two years at us was-born Oksana.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Як ціка́во! Дя́кую, па́ні Гали́но.
lines.source: How interesting! Thank you, Ms. Halyna.
lines.source_literal: How interesting! I-thank, Ms. Halyna.

dialogues.title: The lost phone
dialogues.context: On Sunday Olena meets her brother Taras, who did not answer his phone the day before. They say 'ти' to each other. 'В Андрі́я', at Andrii's, is 'в' with the genitive of a person, which here names that person's place: Andrii's café.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Тара́се, я вчо́ра дзвони́ла тобі́ ці́лий день!
lines.source: Taras, I was calling you all day yesterday!
lines.source_literal: Taras, I yesterday phoned to-you whole day!

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Ви́бач, Оле́но. Учо́ра я втра́тив телефо́н.
lines.source: Sorry, Olena. I lost my phone yesterday.
lines.source_literal: Forgive, Olena. Yesterday I lost phone.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Як? Де?
lines.source: How? Where?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Ура́нці я пив ка́ву в Андрі́я, а по́тім пої́хав на робо́ту.
lines.source: In the morning I had coffee at Andrii's, and then I went to work.
lines.source_literal: In-morning I drank coffee at Andrii, and then went on work.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: На робо́ті я хоті́в подзвони́ти ма́мі, але́ телефо́ну не було́.
lines.source: At work I wanted to call Mom, but the phone wasn't there.
lines.source_literal: On work I wanted to-call to-mom, but of-phone not was.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Ти шука́в його́?
lines.source: Did you look for it?
lines.source_literal: You searched it?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Так, я шука́в його́ дві годи́ни, але́ не знайшо́в.
lines.source: Yes, I looked for it for two hours, but I didn't find it.
lines.source_literal: Yes, I searched it two hours, but not found.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: А де він був?
lines.source: So where was it?
lines.source_literal: And where it was?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Уве́чері я пішо́в до Андрі́я. Як ті́льки він мене́ поба́чив, він сказа́в: «Тара́се, твій телефо́н у ме́не!»
lines.source: In the evening I went to Andrii's. As soon as he saw me, he said, 'Taras, I have your phone!'
lines.source_literal: In-evening I went to Andrii. How only he me saw, he said: 'Taras, your phone at me!'

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Ти забу́в його́ в кафе́?
lines.source: You left it at the café?
lines.source_literal: You forgot it in café?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Так. Я пив ка́ву, говори́в з Андрі́єм і забу́в його́ на столі́.
lines.source: Yes. I was drinking coffee and talking with Andrii, and I left it on the table.
lines.source_literal: Yes. I drank coffee, talked with Andrii and forgot it on table.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: До́бре, що Андрі́й його́ знайшо́в!
lines.source: It's a good thing Andrii found it!
lines.source_literal: Good, that Andrii it found!

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Так. Тепе́р я завжди́ пам’ята́тиму, де мій телефо́н!
lines.source: Yes. From now on I'll always remember where my phone is!
lines.source_literal: Yes. Now I always will-remember, where my phone!

dialogues.title: Sam's biography
dialogues.context: In class, Iryna Petrivna asks each student to tell the story of their life before writing it down. She and Sam say 'ви' to each other. 'Ми з та́том', literally 'we with dad', is the usual way to say 'Dad and I'. 'Хоке́й' is hockey, and 'гра́ти в хоке́й' follows 'гра́ти у футбо́л'.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Се́ме, сього́дні ко́жен пи́ше свою́ біогра́фію. Де ви народи́лися?
lines.source: Sam, today everyone is writing their own biography. Where were you born?
lines.source_literal: Sam, today each writes own biography. Where you were-born?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Я народи́вся й ви́ріс у Кана́ді.
lines.source: I was born and grew up in Canada.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: А що ви пам’ята́єте про своє́ дити́нство?
lines.source: And what do you remember about your childhood?
lines.source_literal: And what you remember about own childhood?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Я пам’ята́ю холо́дні зи́ми. Ко́жної зими́ ми з та́том гра́ли в хоке́й.
lines.source: I remember the cold winters. Every winter Dad and I played hockey.
lines.source_literal: I remember cold winters. Of-every of-winter we with dad played in hockey.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Як ціка́во! А коли́ ви почали́ вивча́ти украї́нську мо́ву?
lines.source: How interesting! And when did you start learning Ukrainian?
lines.source_literal: How interesting! And when you began to-study Ukrainian language?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Коли́ я вступи́в до університе́ту. Я вивча́в її́ протя́гом трьох ро́ків.
lines.source: When I started university. I studied it for three years.
lines.source_literal: When I entered to university. I studied it during three years.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: А що було́ по́тім?
lines.source: And what happened after that?
lines.source_literal: And what was then?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: По́тім я закі́нчив університе́т і знайшо́в робо́ту. А два ро́ки тому́ я пої́хав в Украї́ну.
lines.source: Then I graduated from university and found a job. And two years ago I left for Ukraine.
lines.source_literal: Then I finished university and found work. And two years ago I went in Ukraine.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: І тоді́ ви осели́лися в Ки́єві?
lines.source: And that was when you settled in Kyiv?
lines.source_literal: And then you settled in Kyiv?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Ні, споча́тку я жив у Льво́ві, а зго́дом осели́вся тут.
lines.source: No, at first I lived in Lviv, and later I settled here.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Ду́же до́бре. Тепе́р напиші́ть усе́ це украї́нською за два́дцять хвили́н.
lines.source: Very good. Now write all of that in Ukrainian within twenty minutes.
lines.source_literal: Very well. Now write all this by-Ukrainian within twenty of-minutes.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: За два́дцять хвили́н? До́бре, Іри́но Петрі́вно, я почина́ю!
lines.source: Twenty minutes? All right, Iryna Petrivna, I'm starting!
lines.source_literal: Within twenty of-minutes? Good, Iryna Petrivna, I begin!

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: ви́ріс, дити́нство, пам’ята́ти and the other new words
grammar.explanation:
Every new word in this unit can be read with the rules of the alphabet units and the unit on stress. The points below are the ones that are easy to miss.

A prefix is a short part placed before the root of a verb, and 'ви-' is one of the prefixes that make perfective verbs. In a perfective verb the prefix 'ви-' always takes the stress, in every form: 'ви́рости', to grow up; its future 'ви́росту', 'ви́ростеш'; its past 'ви́ріс', 'ви́росла', 'ви́росли'; and 'ви́грати' from the unit on the conditional. An imperfective verb with the same prefix is stressed elsewhere: 'виро́стати'. A stressed prefix 'ви-' is therefore almost always a sign that the verb is perfective.

'Ви́рости' also changes inside its stem. The 'т' of the future 'ви́росту' appears in neither the infinitive nor the past. In the masculine past the syllable is closed, so its 'о' becomes 'і', as in 'міг', 'могла́': 'ви́ріс' [ˈʋɪrʲis], with the 'р' soft before 'і'. In 'ви́росла' and 'ви́росли' the syllable is open again and the 'о' returns.

'Дити́нство', childhood, is built on the root of 'дити́на', child, with the suffix '-ство', a part added after the root that makes abstract nouns, such as names of a state or a stage of life. It keeps the stress of 'дити́на'. The cluster 'ств' is three consonants in a row: [ˈdɪtɪnstʋɔ].

'Пам’ята́ти', to remember, has the apostrophe after 'м' and before 'я', as 'м’я́со' does. It keeps the 'м' hard and makes the 'я' a full [jɑ]: [pɑmjɑˈtɑtɪ]. The noun it comes from, 'па́м’ять', memory, has the same apostrophe and a soft 'т' at the end.

'Знайти́', to find, builds its forms like 'іти́': the future 'знайду́', 'зна́йдеш' like 'іду́', 'іде́ш', and the past 'знайшо́в', 'знайшла́', 'знайшли́' like 'ішо́в', 'ішла́', 'ішли́'. Its 'й' after 'а' is the 'й' of 'йти'. In 'зна́йдеш' the stress moves to the first syllable.

Consonant changes from earlier units return in the 'я' forms of the new verbs:

- 'т' becomes 'ч' in 'втра́тити': 'втра́чу', as 'леті́ти' gives 'лечу́'.
- 'л' is added after 'п' in 'вступи́ти': 'вступлю́', as in 'куплю́'.
- 'д' becomes 'дж' in 'народи́тися': 'народжу́ся', as in 'ходжу́'. The noun 'наро́дження', birth, of 'день наро́дження', shows the same 'дж'.

The 'в' at the start of 'втра́тити' and 'вступи́ти' stands before a consonant, so it is [w], as in 'вже'. So is the 'в' before 'ся' in the masculine past 'народи́вся', 'осели́вся', 'одружи́вся', as in 'прокида́вся'. 'Втра́тити' also follows the euphony rule for 'у' and 'в', as 'вже' does: after a consonant, after a comma and at the start of a sentence it is written 'утра́тити' ('Він утра́тив ключ.'). 'Вступи́ти' keeps its 'в' everywhere, because 'уступи́ти' is another verb, 'to give way'.

In 'ті́льки', of 'як ті́льки', the soft sign makes the 'л' soft before 'к'. In 'зго́дом' both consonants of 'зг' are voiced, [zɦ]. In 'спо́гад' the final 'д' stays voiced, as every voiced consonant does at the end of a Ukrainian word.

'Мо́лодість', youth, ends in the suffix '-ість', which makes feminine nouns of quality from adjectives: 'мо́лодість' from 'молоди́й'. The noun is stressed on its first syllable and the adjective on its last, so this stress is learned with the word. Nouns in '-ість' keep their 'і' in every form, although the syllable opens: genitive 'мо́лодості', locative 'у мо́лодості'. They are an exception to the alternation of 'кіт', 'кота́'.

In 'біогра́фія' the letters 'і' and 'я' are two syllables, [biɔˈɦrɑfijɑ]: after a vowel, 'я' is [jɑ].

rows: the prefix ви- of a perfective verb
in the closed syllable of the masculine past

grammar.title: Aspect in a story: the line of events and the background
grammar.explanation:
A story in the past has two layers, and Ukrainian shows the layer of each verb by its aspect. The unit on aspect taught what each aspect means; this note shows how a storyteller uses the two together.

The line of events is what happened, one thing after another. Each event is a perfective verb, because each is presented as one completed whole, finished before the next begins. The order of the verbs is the order of the events: 'Вона́ купи́ла квито́к і пої́хала до Льво́ва.', She bought a ticket and set off for Lviv. Swapping the two verbs would change the story.

The background is everything that was going on around the events. Each part of it is an imperfective verb, because it is presented as a process, with no end in view:

- the scene and the weather: 'Ішо́в дощ.', It was raining.
- an activity in progress: 'Я чита́ла кни́гу.', I was reading a book.
- a habit or a repeated action: 'Ко́жного лі́та ми ї́здили до бабу́сі.', Every summer we went to Grandma's.

Two imperfective verbs together describe two actions going on at the same time: 'Ми сиді́ли в кафе́ й говори́ли.', We were sitting in the café and talking. Two perfective verbs together describe two events, one after the other.

An interruption combines the layers. The action that was going on is imperfective, and the event that breaks into it is perfective: 'Я чита́ла, коли́ він узя́в мою́ кни́гу.', I was reading when he took my book. English marks this contrast with 'was reading' against 'took'. Ukrainian has no separate progressive form, so aspect alone does the work.

Aspect also separates trying from succeeding. The imperfective names the effort and the perfective its result, so a perfective with 'не' says that the effort failed: 'Я до́вго шука́в ключ, але́ не знайшо́в.', I looked for the key for a long time but did not find it.

Some storytelling words point to one layer, and others put the events in order:

- 'ра́птом', suddenly, introduces an event, so its verb is perfective.
- 'споча́тку', at first, 'по́тім', next, and 'зго́дом', later, put the events in order.
- 'тоді́' means 'at that time', and in a story also 'then', the next step.
- 'до́вго', 'ча́сто' and 'ко́жного лі́та' describe duration or repetition, so their verb is imperfective.

'Пішо́в дощ' is the perfective 'піти́', to set off, with 'дощ'. It marks the moment the rain began, where 'Ішо́в дощ' describes rain already falling.

In lively spoken stories Ukrainians sometimes switch to the present tense at the most vivid moment, as English speakers do: 'Я сиджу́ в кафе́, і ра́птом Андрі́й ка́же...', I'm sitting in the café, and suddenly Andrii says... Written stories keep the past.

grammar.title: Linking events: коли́, по́ки and як ті́льки
grammar.explanation:
A clause is a part of a sentence with its own verb. A time clause says when the action of the main clause happened, and a conjunction, a joining word, links it to the main clause. Ukrainian writes a comma between the two clauses, and either clause can come first. The three conjunctions of this unit differ in how the two actions fit together in time, and that decides the aspect of the verb in the time clause.

'Коли́', when, takes either aspect, and the aspect shows the relation:

- With an imperfective verb, the two actions overlap: 'Коли́ я жила́ в селі́, я ча́сто гуля́ла бі́ля о́зера.', When I lived in the village, I often walked by the lake.
- With a perfective verb, the action of the time clause was finished first, and the main action followed: 'Коли́ Сем закі́нчив робо́ту, він пішо́в додо́му.', When Sam had finished work, he went home.

'По́ки', while, joins an action that went on for the whole time of the other one, so its verb is imperfective: 'По́ки ма́ма вари́ла борщ, та́то чита́в.', While Mom was cooking borscht, Dad was reading. The main verb is imperfective for a second process, or perfective for one event inside that time: 'По́ки я спав, хтось подзвони́в.', While I was asleep, someone called.

'Як ті́льки', as soon as, says that the main action followed at once, so its verb is perfective: 'Як ті́льки Тара́с знайшо́в телефо́н, він подзвони́в Оле́ні.', As soon as Taras found his phone, he called Olena.

The rule of the unit on the future applies to all three: where English uses the present for a future action in a time clause, Ukrainian uses the future.

- 'Як ті́льки я знайду́ ключ, я тобі́ подзвоню́.', As soon as I find the key, I'll call you.
- 'По́ки ти бу́деш спа́ти, я бу́ду працюва́ти.', While you sleep, I'll work.

One combination means something else. 'По́ки не' with a perfective verb means 'until': 'Я чека́ла, по́ки Тара́с не закі́нчив робо́ту.', I waited until Taras finished work. The word 'не' here negates nothing; the clause names the moment the waiting ended.

grammar.title: How quickly, how long, how much later: за, протя́гом and че́рез
grammar.explanation:
English uses 'in', 'for', 'during' and 'later' for lengths of time, and 'in an hour' can mean two different things. Ukrainian keeps the meanings apart with three prepositions and the accusative alone, and each fits one aspect best.

'За' with the accusative gives the time it took to reach a result, so it goes with a perfective verb: 'Я прочита́в кни́гу за ти́ждень.', I read the book in a week, that is, it took me a week to finish it. 'За' is the preposition of 'за ха́тою', behind the house, with the instrumental, and of 'ви́щий за ме́не', taller than me. With a length of time in the accusative it means 'within'.

A length of time in the accusative with no preposition says how long an action lasted, so it goes with an imperfective verb: 'Я чита́в кни́гу ти́ждень.', I was reading the book for a week, whether or not I finished it. This is the everyday way to say 'for'.

'Протя́гом' with the genitive means 'during' or 'over the course of'. Something went on, or happened again and again, within the period, and the verb is usually imperfective: 'Протя́гом ро́ку я вивча́в украї́нську мо́ву.', Over the course of a year I studied Ukrainian. It belongs mostly to careful speech and writing; everyday speech says 'Я рік вивча́в украї́нську мо́ву.' With 'життя́' it means 'all through one's life': 'протя́гом життя́'.

'Че́рез' with the accusative counts the time until something happens. In the unit on the future it counted from now: 'Я подзвоню́ че́рез годи́ну.', I'll call in an hour. In a story it counts from the moment just told, like English 'later': 'Ми познайо́милися в бе́резні, а че́рез рік одружи́лися.', We met in March, and a year later we got married.

'Тому́' after a length of time in the accusative counts back from now, as the unit on the past showed: 'годи́ну тому́', an hour ago.

So English 'in an hour' is 'за годи́ну' when it says how long something takes, and 'че́рез годи́ну' when it says how long until it happens:

- 'Я зроблю́ це за годи́ну.', I'll get it done within an hour.
- 'Я зроблю́ це че́рез годи́ну.', I'll do it an hour from now.

With a numeral the rules of the units on numerals apply: 'за два дні', 'че́рез п’ять хвили́н', 'протя́гом двох ти́жнів'.

grammar.title: Life events: народи́тися, ви́рости, вступи́ти, одружи́тися
grammar.explanation:
A life story is a chain of events, each told once, so its verbs are mostly perfective. Several of them are reflexive verbs, verbs with the suffix '-ся', and in these verbs '-ся' does not mean 'oneself': it is simply part of the verb. In the past, '-ся' follows the ending for gender and number, as 'прокида́вся' and 'прокида́лася' showed in the unit on the past. The table gives the past of 'народи́тися', to be born.

English says 'I was born', with a form of 'to be'; Ukrainian uses one perfective verb: 'Я народи́вся в Кана́ді.' To someone addressed with 'ви' the plural form is used, for one person as for several: 'Де ви народи́лися?'

The verbs of a life story, in their usual order:

- 'народи́тися', to be born, with 'в' or 'у' and the locative of the place: 'народи́лася в Ки́єві'.
- 'ви́рости', to grow up, also with the locative: 'ви́ріс у селі́'. It is not reflexive.
- 'закі́нчити шко́лу', to finish school, from the unit on aspect.
- 'вступи́ти до університе́ту', to get into a university and begin studying there: 'до' with the genitive.
- 'ста́ти' with the instrumental, to become, from the unit on the instrumental: 'ста́ла лі́каркою'.
- 'одружи́тися', to get married, with 'з' and the instrumental of the partner: 'Мико́ла одружи́вся з Гали́ною.' In the plural it means that two people married each other: 'Вони́ одружи́лися.'
- 'осели́тися', to settle, to make a place one's home, with the locative: 'осели́лися у Льво́ві'.

The dates of a life story use the years of the unit on numerals, where only the last word is an ordinal and takes the locative: 'у ти́сяча дев’ятсо́т дев’яно́сто дев’я́тому ро́ці', in 1999. A person's age at the time is the dative with 'було́': 'Коли́ мені́ було́ сім ро́ків...', When I was seven. A stage of life is 'у' or 'в' with the locative: 'у дити́нстві', in childhood; 'у мо́лодості', in one's youth.

These verbs have imperfective partners ('народжува́тися', 'виро́стати', 'одру́жуватися'), used for a process or a repetition: 'Ді́ти шви́дко виро́стають.', Children grow up fast. A biography tells each event once, so it rarely needs them.

culture.title: Summers at Grandma's, and a writer's childhood
culture.text:
For many Ukrainian families the village is part of the family story. Many city people grew up in a village or still have grandparents there, and city children have long spent their summer vacation, 'кані́кули', at Grandma's, 'у бабу́сі'. The phrase is 'у' with the genitive of a person, which here names that person's home.

Grandparents' memories of village summers return to the same things:

- 'ха́та', the village house, traditionally whitewashed
- the cherry trees by the house: the sour cherry, 'ви́шня', is a symbol of the Ukrainian village, and one of the best-known short poems of the poet Taras Shevchenko opens with a cherry orchard beside a house
- swimming in a lake or a river, picking fruit and helping in the vegetable garden
- long evenings when the family sat together and the old people told stories

The writer Lesya Ukrainka, whose life is told in this unit's first reading, carried her own childhood into her best-known work. She wrote her first poem, 'вірш', at the age of nine; the plural is 'ві́рші'. 'Ле́ся' is the family's affectionate form of the name 'Лари́са', and 'украї́нка' is the word for a Ukrainian woman, so her pen name says 'Lesya, a Ukrainian woman'. She grew up in Volhynia, in the northwest of Ukraine, among forests and lakes, and listened to the songs and legends of the villagers there. Years later, in Georgia, she wrote the play 'Лісова́ пі́сня', 'The Forest Song', about a forest spirit, 'Ма́вка', who falls in love with a young man from a village. Lesya Ukrainka's portrait is on the 200-hryvnia banknote, and Ukrainian pupils read 'Лісова́ пі́сня' at school.

paragraphs.source_literal: I grew-up in village near Poltava. Our house stood near lake, and behind house grew cherries.

paragraphs.target: Ко́жного лі́та, по́ки батьки́ працюва́ли, ми з бра́том ці́лий день гуля́ли бі́ля о́зера і ї́ли ви́шні.
paragraphs.source: Every summer, while our parents were working, my brother and I spent the whole day by the lake eating cherries.
paragraphs.source_literal: Of-every of-summer, while parents worked, we with brother whole day strolled near lake and ate cherries.

paragraphs.target: Одного́ дня, коли́ мені́ було́ сім ро́ків, я пішла́ до о́зера сама́. Я до́вго сиді́ла бі́ля води́, співа́ла й забу́ла про час.
paragraphs.source: One day, when I was seven, I went to the lake on my own. I sat by the water for a long time, singing, and forgot about the time.
paragraphs.source_literal: Of-one of-day, when to-me was seven of-years, I went to lake alone. I long sat near water, sang and forgot about time.

paragraphs.target: Ра́птом пішо́в дощ. Ма́ма шука́ла мене́ протя́гом годи́ни й наре́шті знайшла́ бі́ля о́зера. Як ті́льки ми поверну́лися додо́му, вона́ дала́ мені́ чай із молоко́м.
paragraphs.source: Suddenly it started to rain. Mom looked for me for an hour and finally found me by the lake. As soon as we got back home, she gave me tea with milk.
paragraphs.source_literal: Suddenly went rain. Mom searched me during hour and finally found near lake. How only we returned home, she gave to-me tea with milk.

paragraphs.target: Зго́дом я закі́нчила шко́лу, вступи́ла до університе́ту й осели́лася в Ки́єві. Але́ село́ свого́ дити́нства я пам’ята́ю найкра́ще.
paragraphs.source: Later I finished school, got into university and settled in Kyiv. But the village of my childhood is what I remember best.
paragraphs.source_literal: Later I finished school, entered to university and settled in Kyiv. But village of-own of-childhood I remember best.

questions.prompt: Where did the grandmother grow up?
questions.explanation: 'Я ви́росла в селі́ бі́ля Полта́ви.' She settled in Kyiv only later.

questions.prompt: Why are 'гуля́ли' and 'ї́ли' imperfective in the second paragraph?
choices: They describe what happened again every summer.
questions.explanation: 'Ко́жного лі́та' describes repetition, and 'по́ки' joins two actions going on at the same time, so the verbs are imperfective.

questions.prompt: What happened while the girl was sitting by the lake?
choices: Her brother came to find her.
questions.explanation: 'Ра́птом пішо́в дощ.' The perfective 'пішо́в' marks the moment the rain began and breaks into the background of sitting and singing.

questions.prompt: What did her mother do as soon as they got home?
choices: She gave her tea with milk.
questions.explanation: 'Як ті́льки ми поверну́лися додо́му, вона́ дала́ мені́ чай із молоко́м.' Two perfective verbs: one event followed the other at once.

exercises.prompt: Match each verb with its English meaning
Match each word with its English meaning
Which of these verbs is perfective?
exercises.explanation: 'Знайти́' names the result of a search, one completed whole. 'Шука́ти', 'пам’ята́ти' and 'чита́ти' are imperfective.

exercises.prompt: Why is 'ви́ріс' stressed on its first syllable?
choices: Every past form is stressed on the first syllable.
In a perfective verb the prefix 'ви-' always takes the stress.
The stress mark shows that the verb is imperfective.
exercises.explanation: The prefix 'ви-' of a perfective verb is stressed in every form: 'ви́рости', 'ви́ріс', 'ви́росла', 'ви́грати'. The imperfective 'виро́стати' is stressed elsewhere.

exercises.hint_source: My mom was born in Odesa.
exercises.explanation: 'Народи́тися' is a perfective reflexive verb: '-ся' follows the feminine ending '-ла'.

exercises.hint_source: My dad grew up in a village. Use 'ви́рости'.
exercises.explanation: In the masculine past the syllable is closed, so the 'о' of the stem becomes 'і': 'ви́ріс', but 'ви́росла'.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence tells two events, one after the other?
choices: Сем закі́нчив робо́ту й пішо́в додо́му.
exercises.explanation: Two perfective verbs present two completed events in order. Two imperfective verbs describe actions going on at the same time, and 'ча́сто' describes a habit.

exercises.hint_source: I was reading when Taras called. Use 'чита́ти'.
exercises.explanation: The reading was going on and the call broke into it, so the reading is imperfective: 'чита́в' for a man, 'чита́ла' for a woman.

exercises.prompt_target: Як ті́льки Оле́на ___ робо́ту, вона́ пішла́ додо́му.
exercises.hint_source: As soon as Olena finished work, she went home.
exercises.explanation: 'Як ті́льки' is followed by a perfective verb: one action was complete, and the next followed at once.

exercises.audio_target: Я шука́в ключ, але́ не знайшо́в.
choices: I found the key at once.
I looked for the key but didn't find it.
I left the key at home.

exercises.prompt_target: Я прочита́в цю кни́гу ___ два дні.
exercises.hint_source: I read this book in two days.
exercises.explanation: 'За' with the accusative gives the time it took to reach a result, with a perfective verb.

exercises.prompt_target: Ми познайо́милися в тра́вні, а ___ рік одружи́лися.
exercises.hint_source: We met in May, and a year later we got married.
exercises.explanation: 'Че́рез' with the accusative counts the time from the moment just told until the next event.

exercises.hint_source: Over the course of a year I studied Ukrainian.
exercises.explanation: 'Протя́гом' takes the genitive, 'ро́ку', and says that the studying went on within the period.

exercises.prompt: What does 'Я зроблю́ це за годи́ну.' mean?
choices: I'll do it an hour from now.
I did it an hour ago.
I'll get it done within an hour.
exercises.explanation: 'За годи́ну' is the time needed to reach the result. 'An hour from now' is 'че́рез годи́ну', and 'an hour ago' is 'годи́ну тому́'.

exercises.prompt: Which word fits '___ Окса́на спала́, Тара́с вари́в ка́ву.'?
exercises.explanation: Two actions went on at the same time, both imperfective, so the conjunction is 'по́ки', while. 'Як ті́льки' needs a perfective verb, and 'че́рез' is a preposition, not a conjunction.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means 'Five minutes later Olena called'?
exercises.explanation: 'Че́рез' counts the time until the event. 'Оле́на дзвони́ла п’ять хвили́н.' says how long she was calling, and 'п’ять хвили́н тому́' counts back from now.

exercises.prompt: Which form completes 'Як ті́льки я ___ ключ, я тобі́ подзвоню́.'?
exercises.explanation: The main clause is in the future, and Ukrainian puts the verb of the time clause in the future too: the perfective future 'знайду́', where English says 'as soon as I find'.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'мо́лодість' keep its 'і' in 'у мо́лодості'?
choices: Nouns in '-ість' keep 'і' in every form.
exercises.explanation: The suffix '-ість' keeps its 'і' although the syllable opens, an exception to the alternation of 'кіт', 'кота́'.

exercises.prompt: Sam says 'Ко́жної зими́ ми з та́том гра́ли в хоке́й.' Why is 'гра́ли' imperfective?
choices: 'Ко́жної зими́' describes a repeated action, a habit of his childhood.
exercises.explanation: A habit or repeated action in the past is background, and the background is imperfective.

exercises.prompt: Halyna says 'по́ки я шука́ла для ньо́го кни́гу, він ра́птом запита́в...'. What do the two aspects show?
choices: She was in the middle of looking for a book when his question broke in.
She found the book, and then he asked.
exercises.explanation: 'По́ки' with the imperfective 'шука́ла' is the action going on, and the perfective 'запита́в' with 'ра́птом' is the event that interrupted it.

exercises.prompt: Taras says 'я шука́в його́ дві годи́ни, але́ не знайшо́в.' What does 'не знайшо́в' tell you?
choices: He did not look for it at all.
He searched, but the search had no result.
He found it two hours later.
exercises.explanation: The imperfective 'шука́ти' names the effort; the perfective 'знайти́' with 'не' says that the result never came.

exercises.prompt_source: While I was asleep, someone called.
Two years later we settled in Kyiv.

choices: He talked on the phone for an hour.

exercises.explanation: 'Народи́тися' is one perfective verb, with 'у' and the locative. Before 'льв' the preposition is always 'у'.

exercises.prompt_source: We lived in Lviv for two years.
answers: Ми жили́ у Льво́ві два ро́ки.
Ми два ро́ки жили́ у Льво́ві.
Два ро́ки ми жили́ у Льво́ві.
Ми жили́ у Льво́ві протя́гом двох ро́ків.
Протя́гом двох ро́ків ми жили́ у Льво́ві.
exercises.explanation: How long an action lasted is a length of time in the accusative with no preposition, 'два ро́ки', and an imperfective verb. 'Протя́гом двох ро́ків' says the same in careful speech.

exercises.prompt_source: I read the book in a week.
exercises.explanation: The book was finished, so the verb is the perfective 'прочита́ти', and the time it took is 'за' with the accusative.

exercises.prompt_source: While Oksana was working, Taras was sleeping.
exercises.explanation: Two actions going on at the same time: 'по́ки' with an imperfective verb, and an imperfective main verb.

exercises.prompt: In 'Я чека́ла, по́ки Тара́с не закі́нчив робо́ту.', what does 'не' do?
choices: It negates the verb: Taras did not finish.
Nothing on its own: 'по́ки не' with a perfective verb means 'until'.
It shows that the waiting was in the future.
exercises.explanation: 'По́ки не' with a perfective names the moment the waiting ended: 'I waited until Taras finished work.' Taras did finish.
